h1:
Wat Phra Kaew Kamphaeng Phet
The Big Temple at the Heart of the Old City, and Where Your Walk Begins
intro: Wat Phra Kaew is the main royal temple in the old city of Kamphaeng Phet, set inside the historical park that was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site together with Sukhothai and Si Satchanalai. Walk in and you'll find a wide open courtyard, the base of a large Lanka-style stupa, and a long row of laterite Buddha images. This is where most people start their tour of the old city before fanning out to the other temples. We've put together what to look for, how much it costs, what time it opens, and how to plan a walking route that covers it all in a single morning.
chips: 🛕 Main royal temple of the old city

blocks.html: If you've come to Kamphaeng Phet to see the old city, Wat Phra Kaew is the starting point almost everyone picks, because it sits right inside the walled city area, next to Wat Phra That and the grounds that were once the palace. Its layout is similar to Wat Phra Si Sanphet in Ayutthaya and Wat Mahathat in the centre of Sukhothai — a royal temple inside the palace precinct with no resident monks, used for royal ceremonies. A few steps from the car park and you can already take in the whole temple at a glance.

blocks.text: Why Wat Phra Kaew is the big temple at the city's centre

blocks.html: After the Fine Arts Department excavated the site, they found a single temple holding 35 stupa bases of various styles, 8 viharns large and small, and 3 ordination hall bases. A site this big, with this many structures, tells you straight away that this was a royal temple of real importance to the city. The temple plan is a rectangle laid out parallel to the city wall, and the temple's own wall is built from whole rounded laterite blocks about a metre high — laterite being the main material Kamphaeng Phet's builders used for nearly everything.

Laterite is what gives this city its particular character, unlike Sukhothai which leans on brick. When the afternoon sun hits the porous, orange-brown stone, the colour warms up a lot. Plenty of people say Wat Phra Kaew photographs best in the early morning and late afternoon, because the low-angle light gives the laterite surface some depth.

blocks.text: Three things you have to see at the temple

items.name: The main Lanka-style stupa
items.blurb: A large round Lanka-style stupa stands as the centrepiece of the temple. Lions and elephants once decorated the base, and it's the first thing that catches your eye as you walk in.

items.name: The row of laterite Buddha images
items.blurb: The laterite cores of the principal Buddha and other images sit in a long row. Some still show a hint of the face, others are down to just the base — seeing them lined up makes the scale of the temple click.

items.name: The cluster of stupa bases around it
items.blurb: Thirty-five stupa bases in different shapes are scattered across the courtyard. You can walk around comparing how the base of each style differs — good for anyone who likes the details.

blocks.text: Entry fees, opening hours, and what to know

items: Opening hours — The old city area inside the walls is open daily, roughly 08:00–17:00. The historical park's service desks run on government office hours. Come from morning to late afternoon for good light without too much heat.

Entry fee — Wat Phra Kaew charges separately from the other zones: around 10 THB for Thais and 30 THB for foreigners. A combined park ticket runs about 20 THB for Thais and 100 THB for foreigners (prices may change — double-check at the ticket booth).
Free entry — Seniors aged 60 and over, and students in uniform, get in free.
Dress — This is a historic site with no resident monks, but dress reasonably modestly. Wear comfortable shoes, since the ground is stone courtyard and sand.
No climbing — You can't climb onto the stupa bases or the Buddha images. Shots from ground level already come out great.

blocks.title: A note on light and heat
blocks.html: The temple courtyard is wide open with little shade, and the midday sun is fierce. In the hot season, come before 10am or from about 3pm onward. Bring water and a hat or umbrella. Late afternoon near closing time gives the best light for photographing the laterite.

blocks.text: Start at Wat Phra Kaew, then how to walk the rest of the city

blocks.html: The nice thing about Kamphaeng Phet is that the temples inside the city walls are very close together. Start at Wat Phra Kaew and you can keep walking without getting back in the car. Here's a single-morning route to try.

blocks.label: One morning
blocks.title: Walking the old city, starting from Wat Phra Kaew

items.activity: Enter Wat Phra Kaew and walk around the main stupa and the row of laterite Buddhas
items.note: Soft morning light, nice photos, still few people around

items.activity: Walk on to Wat Phra That right next door and see the square-based stupa and the Buddha niches
items.note: It's in the same walled-city area, less than a five-minute walk

items.activity: Drive or cycle out to the Aranyik zone for Wat Chang Rop and Wat Phra Si Iriyabot
items.note: It's outside the city walls to the north, about 2 km away, and bikes are available to rent

items.activity: Head back into town for lunch — try the egg bananas (kluai khai) or Kamphaeng-style noodles
items.note: The markets and shops in town aren't far from the park

blocks.title: Rent a bike or walk
blocks.html: Inside the city walls you can comfortably walk. But if you want to continue to the Aranyik temple group outside the city, a bike is far more convenient. There are rental spots near the park, and if you drove in you can just park and explore zone by zone on foot.

items: History lovers — You get to see a royal-temple plan from the Sukhothai to early Ayutthaya period, and laterite craftsmanship you don't often come across.
Photographers — The rows of laterite Buddhas and stupas in morning and evening light give you that quiet old-city mood, far less crowded than Sukhothai.
Families and seniors — The ground is fairly flat and easy to walk, seniors enter free, and it's a good spot for a morning stroll.
Travellers passing through — Kamphaeng Phet sits midway between Sukhothai and Nakhon Sawan, so an hour or two walking around Wat Phra Kaew is well worth the stop.

faq.q: What time does Wat Phra Kaew in Kamphaeng Phet open and how much is entry?
faq.a: The old city is open daily, roughly 08:00–17:00. Wat Phra Kaew charges entry separately — around 10 THB for Thais and 30 THB for foreigners. A combined park ticket is about 20 THB for Thais and 100 THB for foreigners. Seniors aged 60 and over and students in uniform get in free. Prices may change, so check again at the ticket booth.

faq.q: How is Wat Phra Kaew in Kamphaeng Phet different from the one in Bangkok?
faq.a: They're different places from different eras. Bangkok's Wat Phra Kaew is the temple inside the Grand Palace that's still in active use. Kamphaeng Phet's Wat Phra Kaew is a historic site in the old city — a royal temple from the Sukhothai period that today is just stupa bases and laterite Buddha images, with no resident monks.

faq.q: How long does it take to walk around Wat Phra Kaew?
faq.a: Wat Phra Kaew on its own takes about 30–45 minutes to cover. But since it's right next to Wat Phra That and close to the other temple groups, most people set aside half a day to walk the old city all together.

faq.q: How do you get to Wat Phra Kaew in Kamphaeng Phet?
faq.a: It's in the town of Kamphaeng Phet, about 4–5 hours' drive from Bangkok, or you can take a coach into town and continue with local transport. The temple is inside the historical park at the centre of town, with a car park and easy bicycle rental for touring the temples.
